Hyperscale data centers already have priority-based load shedding/reduction implemented [7], [8], and in practice the manifestation of the load shedding would be a signal to the IT workload owner, and they would be the one to curtail the lower-priority IT workloads. In this report, we use the multiplier M to simulate the actions of the IT workload owner to execute the load shedding. The total IT load, IT.P, is given as: IT.P=∑IT.P,i∈ {1, . . . ,p} i i The IT load domains have in-line uninterruptible power supply (UPS) to provide momentary power during grid outage events until backup power is restored. The UPS is modeled as a voltage source with a switch- ing logic to transition the load between stable power on the feeder or the UPS. The total cooling load, Cooling.P, is modeled assuming a constant power usage effectiveness (PUE), that is: Cooling.P=(PUE−1)∗IT.P This study uses a PUE of 1.3. The total cooling load is assumed to be split equally across the q cooling domains. The j−th cooling domain’s active power is given by: Cooling .P=Cooling.P/q,j={1,2, . . . ,q}. j Note that constant PUE modeling is assumed for simplicity of the study. In a real scenario, PUE is a function of environmental variables, such as temperature and humidity, which have temporal variations. Additionally, cooling power allocation is not equally spread across the cooling load domains, but for the 5 This report is available at no cost from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) at www.nrel.gov/publications simplicity of the study, it is assumed that the load is equally spread. Power consumption of the cooling air and water movement in the server halls is not considered because it typically represents a small frac- tion (<3%) of the total power consumption. The cooling loads are NOT supported by UPS, and will go through a restart during utility outage and transition to back up power. The total system load, P , in Load the power system is IT.P+Cooling.P.
